title: Descent of a basis consisting of groupoid target pullbacks
statement: Let $U=\operatorname{Spec}A$ and $R=\operatorname{Spec}B$ be affine schemes [def-pc-scheme], [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. Suppose $s,t:R\to U$, $e:U\to R$, $i:R\to R$ and $c:R\times_{s,U,t}R\to R$ [def-pc-fibre-product] are morphisms such that, functorially in every test scheme $H$, $U(H)$ is the object set and $R(H)$ the arrow set of a groupoid with source $s$, target $t$, identity $e$, inverse $i$ and composition $c$. Write $\sigma=s^\sharp,\tau=t^\sharp:A\to B$ and $C=\{a\in A:\sigma(a)=\tau(a)\}$. Let $r\geq1$ and $x_1,\ldots,x_r\in A$. Suppose $\tau(x_1),\ldots,\tau(x_r)$ is a basis of $B$ as an $A$-module via $\sigma$, meaning that every $b\in B$ has a unique expression $\sum_{j=1}^r\sigma(a_j)\tau(x_j)$ with $a_j\in A$. Then $x_1,\ldots,x_r$ is a $C$-basis of $A$, and the ring homomorphism $A\otimes_C A\to B$, $a\otimes a_2\mapsto\sigma(a)\tau(a_2)$, is an isomorphism [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product].

proof.text: Put $\varepsilon=e^\sharp:B\to A$. The identity-arrow laws give $s\circ e=t\circ e=\mathrm{id}_U$: evaluate the assumed groupoid laws on the test scheme $U$ and its identity morphism. Contravariant functoriality on affine spectra gives $\varepsilon\sigma=\varepsilon\tau=\mathrm{id}_A$, so both $\sigma$ and $\tau$ are injective. Also $C$ is a unital subring of $A$: the equality $\sigma(a)=\tau(a)$ is preserved by addition, negation and multiplication, and holds for $1$. Equip $A$ with its inclusion $C\to A$ and $B$ with the common restriction $\sigma|_C=\tau|_C$.

source.place: Tag 03C8 (groupoids-lemma-basis), notation and invariant ring; identity-arrow calculation

proof.text: Let $P=R\times_{s,U,t}R$. The affine fibre-product formula identifies its coordinate ring with $D=B\otimes_{\sigma,A,\tau}B$, where $A$ acts on the first copy of $B$ through $\sigma$ and on the second through $\tau$. Write $p_0(b)=b\otimes1$, $p_1(b)=1\otimes b$, and $\Delta=c^\sharp:B\to D$. Tensor balancing gives $p_0\sigma=p_1\tau$. The source and target laws for composition give $\Delta\sigma=p_1\sigma$ and $\Delta\tau=p_0\tau$: for a composable pair of arrows $(\alpha,\beta)$ with $s(\alpha)=t(\beta)$, the composite $\alpha\circ\beta$ has source $s(\beta)$ and target $t(\alpha)$. These are equalities of scheme maps because the asserted pointwise laws apply to the test scheme $P$ and its pair of projections; take their pullbacks on global sections. Thus no cartesian assertion about the composition map is being assumed.

source.place: Tag 03C8 (groupoids-lemma-basis), first diagram and the formulas preceding its second diagram; composition laws of groupoids-lemma-diagram

proof.text: Apply the free-module base-change statement to the first copy of $B$, free over $A$ through $\sigma$ with the given basis $(\tau(x_j))_{j=1}^r$, along $\tau:A\to B$ into the second copy. Its right-tensor version says exactly that $y_j=\tau(x_j)\otimes1=p_0(\tau(x_j))$ form a basis of $D$ as a module over the second copy of $B$, acting through $p_1$. In particular, if $\sum_jp_1(b_j)y_j=\sum_jp_1(b'_j)y_j$, then $b_j=b'_j$ for every $j$. The two copies of $B$ have different $A$-structures here, and the coefficient ring of this basis is the second copy itself.

source.place: Tag 03C8 (groupoids-lemma-basis), second diagram: the left vertical map is an isomorphism by base change of the middle one

proof.text: Fix $a\in A$, and use the assumed basis to write $\tau(a)=\sum_j\sigma(a_j)\tau(x_j)$ uniquely with $a_j\in A$. Apply $\Delta$ and use step 2 to obtain $p_0\tau(a)=\sum_jp_1\sigma(a_j)y_j$. Applying $p_0$ to the very same expansion and using $p_0\sigma=p_1\tau$ instead gives $p_0\tau(a)=\sum_jp_1\tau(a_j)y_j$. Uniqueness of coefficients in the basis of step 3 yields $\sigma(a_j)=\tau(a_j)$ for each $j$. Hence every coefficient $a_j$ belongs to $C$.

source.place: Tag 03C8 (groupoids-lemma-basis), equalizer comparison in the second diagram, written coefficientwise

proof.text: Apply $\varepsilon$ to the expansion in step 4. Step 1 gives $a=\sum_j a_jx_j$ with $a_j\in C$, proving spanning over $C$. If $\sum_j c_jx_j=0$ with $c_j\in C$, apply $\tau$ to get $\sum_j\sigma(c_j)\tau(x_j)=0$, since $\tau(c_j)=\sigma(c_j)$. The assumed $A$-basis of $B$ says that each $c_j=0$ in $A$, hence in its subring $C$. Thus the $x_j$ are a $C$-basis of $A$.

source.place: Tag 03C8 (groupoids-lemma-basis), the right vertical isomorphism: spanning via the identity section and independence via the given basis

proof.text: The maps $\sigma,\tau:A\to B$ agree on $C$, so the tensor-product ring universal property gives a ring map $\phi:A\otimes_C A\to B$ with $\phi(a\otimes a_2)=\sigma(a)\tau(a_2)$. It is $A$-linear when the source uses the first tensor factor and the target uses $\sigma$. Base change of the $C$-basis in step 5 gives the $A$-basis $(1\otimes x_j)$ of $A\otimes_C A$. The map $\phi$ sends this basis to the assumed $A$-basis $(\tau(x_j))$ of $B$. Explicitly, every $b=\sum_j\sigma(b_j)\tau(x_j)$ is the image of $\sum_j b_j\otimes x_j$; and if $z=\sum_jb_j\otimes x_j$ maps to zero, uniqueness for the target basis gives all $b_j=0$, hence $z=0$. Therefore $\phi$ is bijective, and is an isomorphism of rings. This proves both conclusions with the specified comparison map.
